structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: This document is a notice from HCL Technologies Limited regarding its 33rd Annual General Meeting (AGM) to be held on August 26, 2025, via video conferencing. It includes the AGM notice and annual report for FY 2024-25, sent to stock exchanges and shareholders. The notice covers the adoption of audited financial statements, re-appointment of Ms. Roshni Nadar Malhotra as a director liable to retire by rotation, and re-appointment of Ms. Vanitha Narayanan as an independent director. It also provides company contact details, website, and instructions for accessing the documents online, including for shareholders without registered email addresses.

nodes.title: Item No.3 - Re-appointment of Ms. Vanitha Narayanan (DIN-06488655) as an Independent Director of the Company.

Vijayakumar as Managing Director (designated CEO & Managing Director) from September 1, 2025 to March 31, 2030, liable to retire by rotation, with remuneration effective April 1, 2025. It cites applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, SEBI Listing Regulations, and other rules, subject to Central Government approval and based on Nomination and Remuneration Committee and Board recommendations. nodes.title: Item No.5 -Variation in the HCL Technologies Limited - Restricted Stock Unit Plan 2024.
nodes.summary: The text covers two special resolutions for HCL Technologies Limited. Item No. 5 seeks approval to vary the HCL Technologies Limited - Restricted Stock Unit Plan 2024 by increasing the overall grant limit by 33,00,000 RSUs (from 84,60,000 to 1,17,60,000 RSUs) and increasing the per-employee limit from 13,00,000 to 33,00,000 RSUs, with corresponding equity shares representing up to 0.43% and 0.12% of paid-up capital as on March 31, 2025, respectively, while preserving existing terms and RSU holder interests. Item No. 6 seeks approval for HCL Technologies Stock Options Trust to make secondary acquisitions of up to 33,00,000 equity shares (0.12% of paid-up capital) on recognized stock exchanges, in addition to the previously approved 84,60,000 shares, and for the Board to provide financial assistance (loan, guarantee, security, etc.) to the Trust for this purpose, including additional shares due to corporate actions. Risk owners, typically senior executives, mitigate specific risks, implement strategies, coordinate activities, and ensure information flow. The structure includes the Board's tone at the top, transparent oversight, culture setting, and periodic risk appetite review; the Audit and Risk Management Committees' review of risk management adequacy and monitoring; the RCAC and CRO's leadership in risk initiatives and reporting; the working group's facilitation of ERM practices and mitigation strategies; and risk owners' updates to risk registers and mitigation plans.

Cyber and Resilience risks include information security, business continuity, and geopolitical issues, managed through ISMS, continuity programs, and PESTEL analysis. Governance and Compliance risks encompass ESG, regulatory compliance, privacy, IP management, fraud, and immigration, mitigated by ESG committees, compliance frameworks, privacy systems, IP governance, fraud controls, and immigration groups.

Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements, including the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.

It covers recognition of transaction gains/losses, translation of revenue, expenses, and cash flows at transaction-date rates or weighted averages, translation of foreign operations into INR with exchange differences in OCI, and recognition of OCI on disposal of a foreign operation.

nodes.title: ( e) F a ir v a lue mea surement

It also covers non-recurring fair value measurements for non-financial assets like goodwill and intangible assets, including impairment recognition and the highest and best use concept.

nodes.title: ( f) Rev enue recognition

It addresses multiple-element arrangements with allocation based on standalone selling price, finance lease revenue, gross vs. net reporting for third-party sales, transition services and deferred contract costs, onerous contract provisions, and definitions of contract assets, unbilled receivables, and contract liabilities. nodes.title: Income ta x es
nodes.summary: The text covers income tax accounting, including recognition of current and deferred tax expense in profit or loss or equity, measurement using enacted tax rates, provisions for uncertain tax positions, and offsetting of tax assets and liabilities. It details deferred tax recognition for temporary differences, including those from tax holidays using FIFO reversal, and review and reduction of deferred tax assets. Measurement of deferred tax uses enacted rates, with offsetting under legal conditions. Changes in tax rates are recognized in income or expense. Deferred tax assets are recognized for probable future taxable profits, with exceptions for undistributed subsidiary earnings. Tax benefits from business combinations are adjusted against goodwill or profit or loss. Excess tax deductions from share-based payments are recognized in retained earnings.

It notes that useful lives differ from Schedule II of the Companies Act 2013. For intangible assets, it covers initial measurement at cost (or fair value in a business combination), subsequent measurement at cost less amortization and impairment, amortization over useful lives with a table of asset classes, annual review of amortization periods, and derecognition gains/losses. It also mentions research and development costs, with research expensed and development capitalized when specific criteria are met.

nodes.title: ( k ) Resea rch a nd dev elopment costs
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for research and development costs and borrowing costs. Research costs are expensed as incurred, while development expenditure is recognized as an intangible asset only if the company demonstrates technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete and use/sell, future economic benefits, resource availability, and reliable expenditure measurement. Subsequently, the cost model applies with amortization over expected future benefit and annual impairment testing during development. Borrowing costs directly attributable to qualifying assets are capitalized; all others are expensed. Borrowing costs include interest and other costs incurred for borrowing funds.

nodes.title: ( m) Lea ses

It notes the exemption for short-term leases and the practical expedient to combine lease and non-lease components. The text also addresses the Company as a lessor, distinguishing operating leases (initial direct costs added to carrying amount, contingent rents as revenue) from finance leases (recognized as receivables, lease rentals apportioned between principal and interest, initial direct costs expensed). Finally, it mentions allocation of consideration for contracts with multiple performance obligations.

nodes.title: Inv entories
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for inventories and impairment of non-financial assets. Inventories (stock-in-trade, stores, spares) are valued at lower of cost or net realizable value; cost includes purchase and bringing costs; net realizable value is estimated selling price less completion and sale costs. Cost assignment: specific identification for project-specific stock; weighted average for interchangeable stock and stores/spares. For impairment: goodwill is tested annually or when indicators exist, allocated to cash-generating units (CGUs); impairment occurs when CGU carrying amount exceeds recoverable amount (higher of fair value less costs to sell and value-in-use); impairment losses allocated first to goodwill, then pro-rata to other CGU assets; goodwill impairment not reversed. Intangible assets and property, plant, equipment are tested for recoverability when events indicate possible impairment; recoverable amount determined individually or at CGU level; impairment measured as excess of carrying value over recoverable amount; reversal allowed for changes in estimates, limited to carrying amount that would have existed without impairment, recognized in profit and loss.

nodes.title: P rov isions a nd contingent lia bilities
nodes.summary: The text outlines the accounting policy for provisions and contingent liabilities. It explains that a provision is recognized when a past event creates a present legal or constructive obligation that can be reliably estimated and is probable to require an outflow of economic benefits, with discounting applied if the time value of money is material. It also states that significant judgement is used to disclose contingent liabilities, which are disclosed when a possible obligation exists whose existence will be confirmed by uncertain future events not wholly within the Company's control, or when a present obligation exists but an outflow is not probable or cannot be reliably estimated. Additionally, contingent assets are neither recognized nor disclosed. nodes.summary:
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial repoing and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements include those policies and procedures that (1) peain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements
in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.
